lessons.title: This week's table
lessons.objective: You can read {{team}}'s place in the table and what it needs to achieve.

payload.prompt: The team in fifth has 61 points. {{team}} is fourth with 64. How far ahead are they?

options.text: 5 points
8 points
3 points

explanation.correct: Right. 64 minus 61 is three points. Reading the gap to the team below is the first thing to check in any table.
explanation.incorrect: Fourth on 64 and fifth on 61 means a three-point gap, so one bad result could swap them.
explanation.sayThisLine: We are three clear of fifth, but it is tight.

payload.prompt: {{team}} averages two points a game. Is that title pace?

scene.alt: A team has played 30 games and collected 60 points. That is 2.0 points per game, or about 76 over a 38-game season.

explanation.correct: Right. Two points a game works out at about 76 over 38 games: a strong season, but title winners usually need closer to 2.2 or more.
explanation.incorrect: Two points a game is about 76 over 38 games. That is a very good season, but titles are usually won with roughly 85 or more.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Goals for minus goals against: if you've scored 45 and conceded 30, your goal difference is +15.
explanation.incorrect: Goals scored minus goals conceded: the top tiebreaker when teams are level on points.

payload.prompt: In the Premier League, two teams are level on points. What separates them first?

options.text: Alphabetical order
Goal difference
A coin toss

explanation.correct: Right. The Premier League ranks level teams by goal difference first. Some leagues, such as La Liga, look at head-to-head results first, so it can vary.
explanation.incorrect: Goal difference, goals scored minus goals conceded, is the first tiebreaker in the Premier League. Other leagues can use different rules.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: We are second only on goal difference. One bad afternoon and we drop.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Her team has the same points as the team below but a better goal difference
Goal difference is the only thing that decides the league
She thinks the ranking is unfair
The league has not started yet

payload.translation: Her team is level on points with the side below, and only a better goal difference keeps them ahead. A heavy defeat could swap them.

followUps.line: How many points behind is the top spot?
followUps.why: Moves the chat from the tiebreaker to the bigger race.

followUps.line: Who is the team just below you?
followUps.why: Shows you are following the table.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It is fine to ask her to explain how the table tiebreakers work.

lessons.title: The fixture that matters
lessons.objective: You can explain why this week's match matters and what's at stake for {{team}}.

payload.prompt: {{team}} is one point behind the leader and plays them this week. Why does it matter?

options.text: It is the most glamorous fixture
A win takes them top and beats a direct rival head-to-head
It has the biggest attendance

explanation.correct: Right. In a title race, games against your closest rival are decisive. A win flips the table and takes points away from the team you are chasing.
explanation.incorrect: A win against the leader puts you top, and it stops them from adding points. That is why fans call it a six-pointer.

payload.prompt: Fans say 40 points usually keeps you up. {{team}} has 32 with five games left. How many more?

options.text: 4 points
8 points
12 points

explanation.correct: Right. 40 minus 32 is eight. Forty is only a rule of thumb, and some seasons 36 or 37 is enough, but it is the number fans quote.
explanation.incorrect: Forty minus 32 leaves eight points. Fans use 40 as a safety mark in a 20-team league, though it is not a guarantee.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: It's a derby this week. Form goes out the window.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The usual rankings don't matter in derbies
The match is unpredictable because of the rivalry
One team is too good to lose
Derbies decide the whole season

payload.translation: Derbies between local rivals are so charged with emotion and pride that the better team on paper often doesn't win; rivalries can upset the expected result.

followUps.line: What's the head-to-head record in this derby?
followUps.why: Shows you know derby history matters.

followUps.line: How many of your team's worst losses have come in derbies?
followUps.why: Opens a conversation about the intensity.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You don't need to know the derby history; asking her about it is perfect.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: We play twice in four days and they have a week off. Fixture congestion is brutal.

payload.question: What is she frustrated about?

options.text: Her team gets less rest between games than the opponent
Fixture congestion means lots of matches in a short spell
The match is scheduled too late in the season
Ticket prices are too high

payload.translation: Fixture congestion means many games in a short window. Her team has less recovery time than an opponent who has had a week off, which can hurt legs and rotation.

followUps.line: How many games do you have this week?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Agreeing that a packed schedule is tough is a real, fair observation.

payload.prompt: {{team}} chases the title; their derby rival sits mid-table. What does the rival gain?

options.text: Nothing, the game does not matter to them
A chance to spoil the title chase and win local bragging rights
A trophy for finishing above them

explanation.correct: Right. Even with nothing left to play for in the table, beating a title-chasing local rival can define their season.
explanation.incorrect: A spoiler result against a title contender is huge: three points, bragging rights and a dent in the leader's push.

lessons.title: Injury and lineup news
lessons.objective: You can explain what an injury or lineup change means for {{team}}'s approach this week.

payload.prompt: {{team}}'s main striker is out with a hamstring injury and they play twice in five days. Why is the timing hard?

options.text: It is one-off bad luck; nothing changes
With little recovery time, there is less room to rotate or cover the gap
Two games in five days help him heal faster

explanation.correct: Right. Two games in five days with a key player out means the rest of the squad has to cover more, with less time to rest or reset.
explanation.incorrect: Congestion plus an injury means fewer options and tired legs. That is why the timing hurts.

payload.prompt: Your best centre-back is doubtful. Two games in three days. Do you risk him?

situation.narrative: You are the manager, with a cup match now and a league game against a title rival three days later.

facts.label: Game 2
facts.value: League game vs. a title rival

options.label: Rest him in the cup and let the medical team reassess before the league game
options.consequence: You protect a doubtful player for the bigger game and give the backup minutes.
considerations: Injury risk is higher with little recovery time
The medical staff should have the final say

options.label: Start him in the cup to build match fitness, then review
options.consequence: It can work if he comes through, but a setback would cost you in both games.
considerations: A setback in the cup would hurt the league game too

options.label: Play him in both games regardless
options.consequence: He could be out for weeks if the injury flares up, and the risk lands right before a key fixture.
considerations: Two games in three days with a doubtful player is a big risk

payload.expertNote: Managers weigh how much each game matters, how risky the injury is and how good the cover is, and they lean heavily on the medical team's advice.
payload.sayThisLine: He trained, but the medics say hold him back for the big one.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Doubtful to play. That means he'll probably go, right?

payload.question: Is she right?

options.text: Doubtful means he is very likely to play
Doubtful means he is a genuine question mark and often more likely to miss than to play
Doubtful means the club is not sure, so wait for the team news
Injury news is always obvious

payload.translation: Doubtful sits between "out" and "fit": he is a real question mark and often more likely to miss than to play. Clubs use the word loosely, so wait for the official team news.

followUps.why: That's how you gauge if doubtful means he'll go.

followUps.line: Who plays if he doesn't make it?
followUps.why: Shows you're thinking about the backup plan.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Injury reports are vague by design; teams keep cards close. Asking what the fans think is fair.

payload.prompt: {{team}} has three games in seven days. The manager makes five changes for the second game (a cup match). Why?

options.text: The second game is a chance to rotate and keep legs fresh for the third game
The first game didn't go well
The cup is less important than league matches

explanation.correct: Right. Three games in seven days kills legs; rotating in the less critical game keeps your best players sharp for the league.
explanation.incorrect: Fixture congestion forces rotation. Use the cup match or the least critical game to give regulars a breather.

payload.template: {{status}} means the player is expected to play; {{status2}} means it's uncertain.

explanation.correct: Right. Probable means likely to play. Doubtful means a real question mark. Out means he will miss it.
explanation.incorrect: Probable means trained and likely to start; doubtful means tested but could go either way.

lessons.title: Transfer news decoder
lessons.objective: You can tell rumour from confirmed news and read a 'here we go' moment.

payload.prompt: Transfer news arrives from three places. Which counts as official?

options.text: A tabloid report
A club statement
A forum post that says "trust me"

explanation.correct: Right. A club statement is official. A trusted reporter's "here we go" (Fabrizio Romano is the famous one) usually means a deal is basically done, but the club announcement is the confirmation.
explanation.incorrect: A club statement is the official word. Tabloids and forums are rumour until a club or a trusted reporter confirms it.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: It's deadline day and there's four hours. He's not getting done now.

payload.question: What's her reasoning?

options.text: Medical checks, paperwork and registration take time even on deadline day
The seller is being difficult
Four hours is enough for a complex transfer
Deals cannot be done on deadline day

payload.translation: Late-window deals need medical exams, paperwork, registration and the league's OK; four hours is tight for a big deal unless it's already agreed.

followUps.line: Has the player's club confirmed they agreed a fee?
What's left to do besides medicals?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Deadline day chaos is real; asking why something is stalled is a fair question.

payload.prompt: Contract ends June 30. July 1: he joins anyone free. This move is called?

options.text: A free transfer or out-of-contract move
A loan
A release clause

explanation.correct: Right. When a contract expires, the player is out of contract and can join anyone free of charge.
explanation.incorrect: Contract expiry means the player is free to go. After his contract ends, no club can stop him signing elsewhere without a fee.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Ten different websites say he's done. But no club statement.

payload.question: Should she believe it?

options.text: If many sources agree, it's probably true
Multiple rumours don't equal confirmation; a club or trusted reporter's 'here we go' matters most
Rumours spread faster than facts
One club statement beats ten rumours

payload.translation: Rumours echo across sites even when they're wrong. Only a club statement, a trusted reporter's 'here we go', or official news counts as confirmed.

followUps.line: Has anyone official—club or reporter—said 'here we go'?
Has the player's current club denied it?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rumour season is fun but stressful; staying sceptical is smart.

payload.prompt: Your star winger's contract ends in six months and a big club has bid. What do you do?

situation.narrative: You are the club's sporting director.

options.label: Push for more than €30m, but be ready to accept a fair deal
options.consequence: You use your leverage before he can walk for free, and you keep money to reinvest.
considerations: With six months left, his value is falling every week
A fair fee now beats nothing in the summer

options.label: Accept €30m straight away
options.consequence: You get a fee and move on quickly, but you may leave money on the table.
considerations: You did not test what the buyer would pay

options.label: Keep him until the contract ends
options.consequence: He may leave for free in the summer, and an unhappy player can hurt the team meanwhile.
considerations: A discontented player can drag the squad

payload.expertNote: With a short contract, the seller's leverage shrinks every month. Clubs usually prefer a fair fee now to nothing later.
payload.sayThisLine: He wants out, so thirty million now beats zero in the summer.

lessons.title: Title race and relegation maths
lessons.objective: You can calculate what {{team}} needs from the run-in to win or survive.

payload.prompt: {{team}} has 65 points and three games left. What is the most they can reach?

options.text: 71 points
74 points
77 points

explanation.correct: Right. Three wins would add nine points: 65 + 9 = 74. Working out the maximum is the first step in any title or survival chase.
explanation.incorrect: Three games are worth at most nine points, so the ceiling is 65 + 9 = 74.

payload.prompt: {{team}} is 18th with 25 points. About how many more points would fans call safe?

explanation.correct: Close. About 15 more gets you to 40, the number fans quote as safe in a 20-team league.
explanation.incorrect: Fans use roughly 40 points as the safety mark, so from 25 that is about 15 more. It is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee.

payload.prompt: Fans call a match between two direct rivals a "six-pointer". Why?

options.text: The winner gets six points
A win gains you three and stops your rival gaining three
It counts double in the table

explanation.correct: Right. A win gives you three points and denies a direct rival the chance to take them, so the gap swings by up to six.
explanation.incorrect: The winner still gets three points. It is called a six-pointer because a win also stops your rival collecting three.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: The run-in is brutal. We've got three of the top four coming up.

payload.question: What's she worried about?

options.text: Playing strong teams in the final stretch hurts the title chances
The remaining games are all very difficult
Three games at once
The season is almost over

payload.translation: The run-in is the last set of fixtures; a brutal run-in means tough opponents when {{team}} needs to win. Easy run-ins let you catch up.

followUps.line: What's your worst-case scenario from those three games?
When do you play the bottom half?
followUps.why: Shows you're thinking about winnable games.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Worrying about the fixture list is totally fair; fixture luck is real.

payload.prompt: {{team}} trails by 5 points with 4 games left. If the leader wins all four, how many points would {{team}} need?

explanation.correct: Right. The leader gains 12, so the gap would grow to 17 unless {{team}} got the same. Four games are worth at most 12, so it would be out of reach.
explanation.incorrect: The leader adds 12 points, so to finish level {{team}} would need 5 + 12 = 17. Four games only offer 12, so that is impossible.

lessons.title: What is everyone talking about
lessons.objective: You can name and explain the story fans are talking about today.

payload.prompt: The manager is under pressure after two losses in six games. What do fans mean by 'sack race'?

options.text: A running event for fans
Speculation about whether the manager will be fired
A race to the bottom of the table

explanation.correct: Right. 'In the sack race' means the manager's job is in danger; odds shift as results change.
explanation.incorrect: The sack race is the speculation about which managers might be fired. Media heat rises and falls with results.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: There's an international break next week and three of our best players are away. Nightmare.

payload.question: What's the problem?

options.text: Her team loses match fitness while other teams rest
International matches don't count for the league
Players travel far and come back tired or injured
The league pauses but her team doesn't

payload.translation: International breaks pause the league while national teams play. Her best players are away and often return fatigued or injured, and the club loses time to train together.

followUps.line: Do you have a game right after they get back?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: International breaks are genuinely disruptive; it's a real fixture-list problem.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: VAR checked that for four minutes for nothing. It was never going to change.

payload.question: What's she frustrated about?

options.text: A long VAR review that didn't overturn the on-field call
VAR reviewing an incident that wasn't serious
VAR always makes wrong calls
Four minutes is too long for any review

payload.translation: VAR spent four minutes reviewing and ultimately kept the original call. She feels the review was unnecessary or that the ref should have trusted the on-field read.

followUps.why: Lets her explain what she saw.

followUps.line: Did you think it was the right call in the end?
followUps.why: Invites her to discuss the decision.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Frustration with VAR pace is totally valid; 'clear and obvious' is genuinely subjective.

payload.title: Why is everyone talking about this?
payload.setting: She brings up a story from the past week—maybe a managerial rumour or an injury in an international match.

exchanges.theirMessage: The manager is definitely leaving. Everyone knows it.

replies.text: Has the club said anything? Or is it media speculation?
replies.theirResponse: Speculation so far, but it feels done.

replies.coachNote: Agreeing without facts isn't enough; curiosity matters.
Piling on gives her nothing to talk about, and you have no facts either.

payload.closingNote: Managerial pressure is a huge story; distinguishing rumour from reality helps.

payload.title: Injury during the break
payload.setting: She mentions a player who got injured on international duty and missed her team's next game.

exchanges.theirMessage: He got injured at the international break and now we have to play without him.

replies.text: Ouch. Was it a contact injury or overuse from the extra game?
replies.theirResponse: Tackle. Unnecessary too, the match was decided.
replies.coachNote: Asks for detail and shows empathy.
Sympathy is good; ask for details to show deeper care.

replies.theirResponse: I mean, yeah, but he loves playing for his country.

payload.closingNote: International-break injuries are a sore point; asking details is sympathetic.
